newsitem.title: USA: Colombia proposes controls on oil exports to U.S.
newsitem.headline: Colombia proposes controls on oil exports to U.S.

text.p: Colombia's energy minister Wednesday proposed placing controls on crude oil exports to the United States from Colombia, Mexico and Venezuela, the leading Latin American oil producing countries.

Rodrigo Villamizar, Colombia's Minister of Mines and Energy, stopped short of calling for a Latin American cartel to control production levels, but said the three countries should coordinate export levels to the United States.

"Colombia really thinks that Venezuela, Mexico and ourselves should make joint efforts and coordinate our policies, particularly of oil exports in the future, particularly in relation to the United States," Villamizar said.
The proposal comes as President Clinton considers imposing punitive sanctions on Colombia after decertifying the country last year for falling short in its war on drugs.

A decision on renewing the decertification for a second year is due by March 1, and could trigger U.S. commercial sanctions against Colombia as that country courts foreign investment to boost oil production and privatise its electric industry.

Colombia's proposal, made during a Latin American energy summit in Houston, met a chilly reception from energy ministers of Venezuela and Mexico, which combined account for nearly a third of U.S. petroleum imports.
"I think that the wording is not very fortunate," Mexico Energy Minister Jesus Reyes Heroles said of Colombia's call to coordinate export policies of the three Latin American countries.
"That would not be the way to go, and we would not participate in that," said Luis Giusti, president of Petroleos de Venezuela SA, which has been steadily expanding its exports to the United States.

The Venezuelan state-owned oil company is in talks with several U.S. refiners on ventures to upgrade Gulf Coast refineries to handle its heavy crude oil in return for a share of production and retail profits downstream.

Venezuela is the leading petroleum exporter to the United States, supplying about 1.6 million barrels per day or more than 17 percent of total imports, while Mexico was the fourth leading importer at 1.23 million barrels per day.

Colombia, meanwhile, is seeking to boost production by a third to about 920,000 barrels per day by next year and build reserves to 15 billion barrels in the next 50 years, up from 3.5 billion barrels today.

Latin American countries have been striving in recent years for increased hemispheric cooperation, which in the energy industry has led to electric power lines being strung across borders and investment aimed at producing abundant natural gas reserves for regional consumption.
By teaming up with Venezuela and Mexico, Colombia might be seeking to boost its standing in the world oil community and bolster Latin America's role as a key U.S. supplier, analysts said.

"(The proposal) can be an attempt to command higher prices, and it's a very subtle way to collude, which I don't think is in the interst of the U.S. And I don't think it is in the interest of the market either," Guillermo Guariguata, president of Houston consulting firm Bonner & Moore Associates said.
